title: Treble crochet
subtitle: The tall everyday stitch, called double crochet in the United States
excerpt: The treble is the tall workhorse of crochet. Three yarn-overs and three pulls make a post about twice the height of a double crochet. It builds lacy, open fabric quickly, which is why most edgings, motifs, and blankets lean on it.
sourceNotes: Reconstructed in our own words from Thérèse de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Chapter 9 (Crochet Work), the passage on trebles worked one above another (Fig. 416). Public domain via Project Gutenberg. UK and US stitch-name equivalences cross-checked against the Craft Yarn Council standard terms.

glossaryTerms.definition: A tall crochet stitch made with one yarn-over before the hook goes in, then worked off in two steps. About twice the height of a double crochet. The UK name; the same stitch is called double crochet in the United States.
The United States name for the stitch British patterns call a treble. The action is identical; only the name differs, which is the most common UK and US crochet mix-up.
Wrapping the working yarn over the hook from back to front before working a stitch. Each wrap adds height; a treble takes one wrap before the hook goes in.
The single live loop that sits on the hook between stitches. Every stitch begins and ends with one working loop on the hook.

content.text: The
treble
is the tall, quick stitch that most crochet leans on. You make it with one
yarn round hook

before the hook goes in, then work the loops off in two steps. The finished post stands about twice as tall as a double crochet, so the fabric grows fast and sits open and soft. In the United States this exact stitch is called
double crochet
, which trips up many a reader crossing between British and American patterns.

content.text: How to form the stitch
Start with one
working loop
on the hook and a foundation chain or a row of stitches to work into.
Wrap the yarn over the hook once, from back to front.
Insert the hook into the next stitch or chain space.
Catch the yarn and draw a loop back through. Three loops now sit on the hook.
Wrap the yarn over the hook again. Pull it through the first two loops. Two loops remain.
Wrap the yarn over once more. Pull it through the last two loops. One loop is left, and the treble is done.
At the start of a row or round, three chains stand in for the first treble, because the post is three chains tall.
Where you will use it

The treble is the building block of granny squares, openwork blankets, shawls, and most crochet edgings. Worked in clusters of three into one space it makes the classic granny fan. Worked one into each stitch it gives a quick, soft fabric good for wraps and light blankets. Where you want height and drape without a dense surface, the treble is the stitch you reach for.
Variations and related stitches

Shorten the treble by one step and you get a half treble, which is firmer and a touch shorter. Add a second yarn-over at the start and you get a double treble, which is taller again. Work two trebles together at the top and you have a decrease; work three into one space and you have a cluster. The treble sits in the middle of the family of posts, and once your hands know it the taller and shorter stitches follow the same rhythm.
Difficulty: beginner. The treble is usually the second stitch a new crocheter learns, after the double crochet, and the one most patterns assume you can work.
